questions.prompt: Which of these does YouTube say needs no AI disclosure?

options.text: A clip that makes a real person say something they never said
options.explanation: YouTube lists this as content that must be disclosed.

options.text: Using AI to improve a video title, a thumbnail or a script
options.explanation: Right. YouTube lists production assistance, such as improving a script, thumbnail or title, as needing no disclosure.

options.text: Realistic extra footage of a real place that was never filmed
options.explanation: YouTube lists AI footage of a real place as content that must be disclosed.

questions.prompt: In May 2024, what did TikTok say it could do with Content Credentials?

options.text: Read them, so it can label AI content made on other platforms
options.explanation: Right. TikTok said it was launching the ability to read Content Credentials to auto-label AI-generated content from some other platforms.

options.text: Remove them from every upload, so that all files look the same
options.explanation: TikTok said it would read them, and later attach them to its own content.

options.text: Ignore them, because TikTok only labels what creators tell it
options.explanation: TikTok said creators must label realistic AI content, and that it also reads Content Credentials.

questions.prompt: What does the European Commission's page say about its Code of Practice and Article 50?

options.text: Both are voluntary, so that a brand can choose to skip either of them
options.explanation: Only adherence to the code is voluntary. The Article 50 requirements are legal obligations.

options.text: The code is voluntary, but the Article 50 requirements are legal obligations
options.explanation: Right. The page says that even though adherence to the code is voluntary, the Article 50 requirements are legal obligations.

options.text: The code is binding law, while Article 50 is only a loose suggestion
options.explanation: It is the other way round. The code is a voluntary tool.
